演奏班卓琴以撥弦發聲，琴弦振動經張於琴框或琴腔的薄膜與木製共鳴器傳導。初學可先確: The banjo is played by plucking, the vibration of the strings passing through the membrane stretched over the frame or the resonator and through the wooden resonator. A beginner should first settle the number of strings and the tuning: the traditional five-string is the most common and four-string is also general; the six-string version is tuned and played like a guitar, so a grounding in guitar carries over. The sound is usually made by plucking, or by rolling arpeggios with the right hand that set the strings vibrating one at a time or together.

班卓琴以撥弦振動張於琴框的薄膜發聲，膜面振動使音色短促、明亮，並帶有打擊感。傳統: The banjo sounds by plucking strings whose vibration is passed to the membrane stretched over the frame; the membrane's vibration makes the timbre short and bright with a percussive edge. The traditional goatskin membrane and the modern polyester one affect the overtones and the brightness. The volume is not great, and the wooden resonator behind the body spreads the sound outwards, improving the tone and the volume. It is mostly played by plucking or by right-hand arpeggios that control the force and the rhythm, and the timbre is drier than a fiddle's, which suits bluegrass, old-time music, Dixieland jazz and Caribbean music.
班卓琴常見於巡迴黑臉滑稽戲、家庭客廳音樂娛樂、大學音樂俱樂部與二十世紀早期爵士樂: The banjo is common in travelling blackface minstrel shows, in parlour music at home, in university musical clubs and in early twentieth-century jazz bands, and it survives in rural folk culture. It was later mostly associated with folk music, blues, cowboy music, country music, old-time music and bluegrass, often played with the fiddle; it also appears in Dixieland jazz and in Caribbean music such as calypso, mento, bélé and tumba. Early on, in North America and the Caribbean, it was played for idle pastime, at parties, at kalinda gatherings and at funerals.

The banjo is a plucked lute-type chordophone, number 321.322-8. Its body has a round membrane over a frame or resonator, in modern instruments mostly polyester film and early on goatskin; it is played by plucking, or with right-hand arpeggios. It was developed by African Americans, reached the American and British public through travelling shows, and appears in rural folk music, the home parlour, university clubs, early jazz, bluegrass, country, Dixieland jazz and Caribbean music, and occasionally in rock, pop and hip-hop.
班卓琴源自17世紀北美與加勒比被奴役的西非、中非人所用的葫蘆共鳴撥弦樂器，早期以: The banjo comes from the gourd-resonated plucked instruments played by enslaved West and Central Africans in seventeenth-century North America and the Caribbean; the early ones were made from a halved gourd, animal skin, a wooden neck and gut or plant-fibre strings. A document from Martinique in 1678 mentions the banza, and in 1621 Richard Jobson described a similar instrument in the Gambia. In the nineteenth century it spread through the United States and Britain with the blackface minstrel show, and mass production, mail order and tutors brought it into the home parlour, university music clubs and early jazz. Joel Walker Sweeney is credited with adding a string and promoting the five-string, and in the 1830s it passed to the first white performers. After the twentieth century it has been closely associated with folk, blues, country and bluegrass music.
